Although the classical generation of arbitrary IQP randomness is believed to be hard,
many other properties of IQP circuits can still be efficiently simulated.
Among them, a particularly simple one is the estimation of Pauli-$X$ averages.

::: {#lem-iqp-x-pauli-average .callout-important icon="false"}
## X-Pauli Average Estimation

For any efficiently specified IQP circuit with diagonal part $D$, there is a $\mathsf{BPP}$ algorithm that estimates the Pauli-$X$ expectation value
$$
\mu_s = \bra{0}_X D^\dagger X^s D \ket{0}_X
$$
to additive error $\varepsilon$ with success probability at least $1-\delta$, using
$$
N = \frac{2}{\varepsilon^2}\ln\frac{2}{\delta}
$$
samples. In particular, Pauli-$X$ averages of IQP circuits admit a classical randomized constant-error estimator.
:::

For a given IQP circuit, write its diagonal unitary as $D$. By diagonality,
$$
\bra{x}D\ket{y} = f(x)\delta_{x,y},
$$
where, for each fixed input $x$, the phase
$$
f(x) = \bra{x}D\ket{x}
$$
is efficiently computable from the circuit description. Let $\ket{x}_X$ denote the simultaneous eigenvector of the Pauli-$X$ operators, with eigenvalue $(-1)^{x_i}$ under $X_i$. Then
$$
\begin{align}
\bra{0}_X D^\dagger X^s D\ket{0}_X
&= \sum_u \bra{0}_X D^\dagger \ket{u}_X
   \bra{u}_X D \ket{0}_X (-1)^{u\cdot s} \\
&= 2^{-2n}\sum_{l,m,u}
   \bra{l}D^\dagger\ket{l}(-1)^{u\cdot l}
   (-1)^{u\cdot m}\bra{m}D\ket{m}(-1)^{u\cdot s} \\
&= 2^{-2n}\sum_{l,m,u}
   f^*(l)f(m)(-1)^{u\cdot(s+l+m)} \\
&= 2^{-n}\sum_l f^*(l)f(l+s),
\end{align}
$$
where all additions in the bit strings are over $\mathbb{F}_2^n$.

Therefore the sum over $l$ can be estimated by sampling $l$ uniformly from $\{0,1\}^n$ and averaging the efficiently computable quantity
$$
Y_l = f^*(l)f(l+s).
$$
The mean of this random variable is exactly $\mu_s$. Since the Pauli expectation value is real, we may output the real part of the empirical average; the sampled real values are bounded in $[-1,1]$. By Hoeffding's inequality,
$$
\Pr\!\left[|\hat{\mu}_s-\mu_s|>\varepsilon\right]
\leq 2\exp\!\left(-\frac{2N\varepsilon^2}{2^2}\right).
$$
Taking
$$
N = \frac{2}{\varepsilon^2}\ln\frac{2}{\delta}
$$
makes this failure probability at most $\delta$. Thus the Pauli-$X$ average can be estimated to additive error $\varepsilon$ with confidence $1-\delta$ by a randomized classical algorithm running in polynomial time.
